China’s top diplomat told his Cuban counterpart on Wednesday that Beijing would “firmly support” Havana in opposing sanctions, as the island came under fresh restrictions from Washington.
The United States has launched devastating sanctions and an oil blockade against Cuba since January, crippling its economy and triggering widespread blackouts and shortages of necessities.

articles.title_orig: Iran War Updates: Iran vows not to part with "single particle of enriched nuclear material" as standoff continues
articles.title_zh: Iran War Updates: Iran vows not to part with "single particle of enriched nuclear material" as standoff continues
articles.content_orig:
Iranian security chief Mohsen Rezaei threatened to strike U.S. bases beyond the Middle East, including in Europe, if they are used for attacks against the Islamic Republic.
"If American aircraft take off from an American military base, even one located in a European country or some other distant region, to bomb Iran, we will strike those bases as well," Rezaei told Lebanon-based Al Mayadeen TV in an interview broadcast Wednesday.
In a "60 Minutes" interview that aired Sunday, President Trump said he does not currently see "any reason" to escalate the war.
Rezaei also said that Iran's response to renewed U.S. attacks would "target America's more distant military installations — including the ones we have not yet attacked," without specifying.
"We may even strike certain islands that they assume are beyond the reach of our missiles," he added during the interview, which was conducted in Tehran.
The Saudi-led coalition fighting Yemen's Houthis said on Wednesday that it shot down three cruise missiles fired at Riyadh, which has been targeted for weeks by the Iran-backed group.
"Air defenses intercepted and destroyed 3 cruise missiles launched by the Houthi terrorist militia toward the Riyadh area," coalition spokesperson Turki al-Malki posted on social media.
The latest incident comes after the Houthis damaged a skyscraper belonging to oil giant Saudi Aramco in the capital's gleaming financial district on Sunday.
Riyadh's international airport has also been targeted repeatedly, with deadly attacks forcing it to close for two weeks last month.
Saudi Arabia formed an international coalition to fight the Houthis in 2015, after the group's takeover of Yemen's capital Sanaa.
After years of an uneasy truce, the conflict reignited in July.
Iran's Defense Ministry on Wednesday rejected Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth's latest blustery assessment of Tehran's military capacities, calling his depiction a fabrication and insisting Iranian armed forces still had weapons stockpiled.
Iran's weapons stockpile "far exceeds the deceptive figures fabricated by Trump and the defeated Pete," a ministry spokesperson said, adding that the country had made use of "strategic production and upgraded technologies."
Hegseth told reporters Tuesday that during 40 days of combat, the U.S. had struck 13,000 targets, destroying, he said, more than 80% of Iran's nuclear industrial base.
"Their navy sunk, their air force grounded, their defense industrial base gone," Hegseth said.
Iranian officials claimed a month ago that the country's weapons production capacity had increased by 250% since the war began, with help from Russia and China.
Neither side has offered evidence to prove their claims, and neither the U.S. nor Iran have launched large-scale strikes since the summer. Both claim to have won the war, but despite Hegseth's assertion on Tuesday that the Strait of Hormuz is under U.S. control, Iran continues attacking vessels daily in and near the waterway.
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has relocated from his home in the Washington, D.C., area to a military base following a series of Iranian threats against his life.
"The secretary will not be deterred by the Iranian regime's threats and remains committed to executing Operation Economic Outcast and maintaining the blockade, which together are collapsing Iran's economy," a Treasury Department spokesperson said.
A source familiar with the situation pointed to a Wall Street Journal story as the impetus for the move.
"After The Wall Street Journal published an article featuring an online photo that allowed the location of the secretary's Georgetown home to be geo-located, security concerns began to increase which have now forced the secretary to relocate to a military base for his safety," the person told CBS News.
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian accused the U.S. on Wednesday of threatening to attack his country with America's largest non-nuclear weapon — the "mother of all bombs" — while claiming to seek a diplomatic resolution to the war.
In a post on X , Pezeshkian criticized the U.S. for what he called an effort to "pursue diplomacy through threats."
"No contradiction but a disgrace. Who threatens global peace and security?" he wrote.
CBS News reported in October that the White House and Pentagon had prepared plans to use the Massive Ordnance Air Blast Bomb, or MOAB — an acronym that has earned it the nickname used by Pezeshkian —   to hit military sites in Iran if President Trump were to give the order, according to sources familiar with the matter.
The MOAB is the largest non-nuclear weapon in the U.S. arsenal, weighing upwards of 30,000 pounds. Mr. Trump set a precedent for its use in 2017, when it was deployed to attack an ISIS cave complex in Afghanistan. It is designed to destroy infrastructure buried deep underground.
An adviser to Iran's supreme leader said Wednesday that the U.S. and Europe "have heard the repercussions" of the war launched jointly more than eight months ago by the U.S. and Israel.
In a post on X, Mohammad Mokhber said other nations' participation in the U.S. blockade of Iranian ports constituted an act of war that would be recorded "in the nation's historical memory."
"Responsibility and the consequences of such actions will extend to all participants, regardless of geographical boundaries," Mokhber said.
He did not mention any specific repercussions, but France has blamed Iran for nationwide cyberattacks that hit commercial refrigeration units at hundreds of grocery stores in October, spoiling thousands of tons of food and causing at least 20 fires, according to French prosecutors.
In September, U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Iran was believed to have "played a part" in a security incident near an air base in England that had been used by U.S. forces to launch strikes on Iran.
Iran-linked groups have also been accused of backing a series of sabotage attacks in the U.K. and Europe, including many targeting Jewish communities.
Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said Wednesday that two more oil tankers had struck sea mines and caught on fire in the Strait of Hormuz, the latest of what have become daily claims by Iranian forces about attacks on commercial vessels in and around the strategic waterway.
"Two oil tankers that attempted to secretly leave the Strait of Hormuz last night via an unauthorized and hazardous route, under the protection of fighter jets belonging to the plundering and aggressor U.S. military, struck naval mines and sustained massive explosions," the IRGC said in a statement.
Iran has attacked ships for months that it accuses of trying to transit the waterway without its approval, using southern shipping lanes the U.S. military insists are safe and open . The U.S. military, meanwhile, has also struck tankers it accuses of violating its blockade of Iranian ports.
The IRGC claimed Tuesday that at least two oil tankers had caught on fire after explosions in the strait under similar circumstances, and the U.K. navy's Maritime Trade Operations center said a tanker reported being hit by a projectile in the strait on Tuesday evening.
The U.S.-Iran war will cost Gulf countries more than $200 billion in damage and economic losses could reach nearly four times that amount by 2030, insurer Allianz Trade said on Wednesday.
Gulf countries which hosted U.S. forces came under attack on a daily basis in the opening weeks of the war as Iran retaliated against U.S. and Israeli attacks.
"Physical damage across the region is assessed just above $200bn, mostly concentrated in Hormuz-locked economies, especially in energy infrastructure," the insurer said in a report.
More than 80 energy facilities were hit in the war, mostly in Kuwait, Qatar and Bahrain, the report said, with a third of them "severely damaged."
Beyond physical damage to energy infrastructure, the war has affected other sectors like tourism and real estate, which will see slower growth over the years.

articles.title_orig: Hadean mantle depletion and 3.95-Gyr subduction implied by North China rocks
articles.title_zh: Hadean mantle depletion and 3.95-Gyr subduction implied by North China rocks
articles.content_orig:
Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain
            the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in
            Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles
            and JavaScript.
The scarcity of terrestrial rocks older than 3.9 billion years (Gyr) has hindered our understanding of Earth’s early evolution, fuelling persistent debates on how and when the first continental crust formed and plate tectonics started. At present, the only unequivocally documented >3.9-Gyr-old rocks are from the Acasta Gneiss Complex, Canada 1 , 2 , 3 . Here we report a 3.95-Gyr-old trondhjemitic gneiss from eastern Hebei, North China Craton, in which primary magmatic zircon records elevated δ 18 O values (average +6.77 ± 0.23‰) and positive ε Hf ( t ) values (weighted mean +1.45 ± 0.27). This suggests a low-temperature altered basaltic source that originated from a mantle depleted in the Hadean. In contrast to the low-pressure origin inferred for the roughly 4.0-Gyr-old Idiwhaa unit in Acasta 2 , the 3.95-Gyr-old trondhjemitic gneiss reported here exhibits geochemical signatures attributed to a high-pressure origin 4 . Thermodynamic and trace element modelling demonstrate that its parental magma formed by means of low-degree (8–16%) melting of basaltic crust at >1.6 GPa and 740–820 °C, suggesting rapid burial of (near-)surface-altered oceanic crust to mantle depths along a cool thermal gradient. We propose that this rapid burial was most likely achieved through a transient subduction event.

Boeing and Google already have spots at the Apec CEO Summit confirmed, but Nvidia likely to be absent, source says
Representatives from Google and Boeing will be included in the United States’ business delegation at next week’s Apec CEO Summit in Shenzhen, the event organiser has confirmed.
But a source familiar with the arrangements said Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang was unlikely to attend at this stage, with many high-profile executives yet to confirm their participation.
The China Council for the Promotion of International Trade (CCPIT), the summit’s organiser, said Google, Boeing, UBS and the Thai conglomerate Charoen Pokphand Group were among the companies that had already applied to attend the meeting, according to a report by state broadcaster CCTV on Wednesday.

articles.title_orig: Veterans Day 2026 brings free meals at popular restaurants — and some deals don't end Nov. 11
articles.title_zh: Veterans Day 2026 brings free meals at popular restaurants — and some deals don't end Nov. 11
articles.content_orig:
Veterans Day, observed annually on November 11, honors Americans who have served in the U.S. military. Formerly known as "Armistice Day," the holiday was celebrated nationally for the first time in 1919 at the direction of former U.S. President Woodrow Wilson. Congress officially recognized it as a federal holiday in 1926.
This year, Veterans Day falls on a Wednesday. Read on to see which businesses are operating and some of the deals they are offering veterans and active military members to thank them for their service.
Most major grocery chains are open, including Aldi, Food Lion, Publix, Stop & Shop, Trader Joe's, Wegmans and Whole Foods.
Walgreens confirmed that it will welcome customers on Wednesday. CVS locations will be open, although some stores and pharmacies may have reduced hours, a spokesperson said.
Other retailers are also generally open on Veterans Day, although it's a good idea to check your local retailer's hours ahead of time.
The big-box store will be open for Veterans Day, according to its holiday schedule .
Target stores will be open on Wednesday during regular business hours, a company spokesperson confirmed.
Walmart stores will operate during their regular hours on Veterans Day, according to a company spokesperson.
Major banks such as Bank of America, Chase and TD Bank are closed on Wednesday, as Veterans Day is a federal holiday observed by the Federal Reserve.
Americans can still visit ATMs and check online account activity. However, the holiday may affect the time it takes to process certain transactions, Bank of America says on its website .
All post office locations will be closed, and mail will not be delivered on Wednesday due to the federal holiday. Mailing and retail services will resume on Thursday, Nov. 12, according to the USPS .
The U.S. stock market will be open, with Veterans Day not among the holidays observed by the New York Stock Exchange and Nasdaq. The next time markets will be closed is on Thanksgiving, which falls on Thursday, Nov. 26.
Here are a few discounts and freebies retailers are offering on Tuesday to veterans and active service members. Be prepared to show your military identification.
More deals can be found on the American Legion's website .

articles.title_orig: Megaspeed's vacant offices raise questions about ties to Nvidia and China
articles.title_zh: Megaspeed's vacant offices raise questions about ties to Nvidia and China
articles.content_orig:
The unusual global footprint of Megaspeed International, the Singapore-based company at the center of the Nvidia Chinese spy scandal, is fueling questions about whether it's a front for the Chinese government.
One of Megaspeed's leaders is Alice Huang, the woman with whom Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang was having an affair, and who is suspected by U.S. intelligence of being an asset of China's Ministry of State Security . In the past three years, Megaspeed, formerly a gaming company, has been one of Nvidia's biggest foreign customers, purchasing nearly $5 billion in AI chips and advanced hardware, The New York Times first reported.
And yet Megaspeed's corporate headquarters sat practically empty, according to The Straits Times, an English-language newspaper in Singapore. Questions have also been raised about its outposts in Australia and Malaysia.
Published reports in recent days revealed that the company listed a newspaper vendor as the director of its Australian subsidiary, and one of its Malaysia offices consisted of a dilapidated storefront outside Kuala Lumpur. Yet another Malaysia office was tucked into a shopping mall.
Megaspeed began as an offshoot of a China-based gaming firm and grew into a juggernaut by gaining access to restricted Nvidia AI computer chips. U.S. investigators say that Alice Huang used her contacts in the industry and a series of shell companies to gain access to 240,000 chips banned for export into China. Now it is being probed in both the U.S. and Singapore for allegedly smuggling those chips into China.
President Trump said this week the FBI is also investigating romantic and business ties between Nvidia's chief executive Jensen Huang and Alice Huang (who are not related).
Earlier this week, Jensen Huang, who is married, apologized for the affair in a statement to Nvidia's employees. The company launched an independent investigation of the matter , and an Nvidia shareholder filed a class action lawsuit Tuesday alleging that Huang concealed a relationship with Alice Huang and misled shareholders about national security concerns raised by the relationship.
Nvidia's board said it had no reason to believe that the company's secrets or national security were compromised.
"The Board prioritizes U.S. national and economic security, which is paramount to the interests of NVIDIA and its shareholders," its statement said.
China expert Jacqueline Deal said that Nvidia's advanced AI chips could have ended up with the Chinese military. Deal, who is an adviser to State Armor, a nonprofit that studies global security threats, told CBS News, "If allegations are true, who will be fired? Nvidia has a compliance team that may have failed utterly."
She also questioned the effectiveness of the U.S. Commerce Department, which has jurisdiction over export controls that may have been bypassed, potentially giving the Chinese military access to the world's most advanced chips.
Here's what we now know about Megaspeed:
It is a major Nvidia customer. Megaspeed and its Malaysian affiliate, Speedmatrix, purchased $4.8 billion of Nvidia's advanced artificial intelligence equipment and processors over the last three years.
In 2025, Megaspeed International faced an investigation by Singapore police for alleged breaches of local laws, but no details have emerged about the probe, according to The Straits Times.
"Megaspeed International is a premier business partner of NVIDIA, strategically positioned in the Asia Pacific region," according to its LinkedIn profile, which claims it has between 201 and 500 employees. Three years ago it listed between two and 10 employees, according to the South China Morning Post.
Megaspeed International did not reply to a request for comment. It posted an "official statement" on its website addressing what it called "misleading information" and "incorrect insinuations" accusing it of involvement in illegal chip transfers.
"We want to be absolutely clear over the past six months our company has undergone multiple on-site inspections and reviews by key institutions, including the Bureau of Industry and Security of the US Commerce Department, the Ministry of Investment, Trade and Industry of Malaysia and NVIDIA," said the message, which also appeared on the company's LinkedIn page.
"These thorough investigations have confirmed that there has been no evidence of any violations concerning the illicit transfer of chips or any illegal activities," the company said.
Megaspeed was originally incorporated in 2015 under the name 7Road International, a subsidiary of a Chinese developer of popular video games and mobile apps based in Shenzhen, China, according to corporate filings.
Huang Le Limited, a shell company in the British Virgin Islands, acquired 7Road International in March 2023. Huang Le is the Chinese name of Alice Huang.
That same month, 7Road International was renamed Megaspeed International, and Huang became its managing director. The company also launched a subsidiary called Speedmatrix.
By the end of October 2023, Huang and another Megaspeed director, Cang Yang, resigned from the company after it was bought up by a firm called Swiftdata, whose director is based in China, documents show.
But there's some indication Huang may still be affiliated with the company. Culper Research, an activist short-selling firm, published a 40-page report on Nvidia in May that cited Megaspeed employees who said Huang was still running the company.
The report also raised some concern about Jensen Huang's relationship with Megaspeed and Alice Huang, stating, "Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has not only vouched for Megaspeed, but seems to have quite literally walked alongside Megaspeed at every step, while maintaining an uncomfortably close relationship with Megaspeed's Alice Huang, a Chinese national."
Megaspeed lists its headquarters office address on the seventh floor of the Ocean Financial Centre in Singapore, a glass office tower in Singapore's central business district.
When the Straits Times and The New York Times visited the Singapore offices around the same time late last year, they found little or no staff working. The Straits Times said the door was locked, and the Times found just two people in its office on a workday.
Megaspeed has an Australian subsidiary on the 10th floor of a commercial and retail tower in the heart of Sydney's central business district. Forty other businesses are on the same floor, and space in the building can be rented for as little as $17 per day, Australia's ABC News reported. Corporate filings name Shanghai-born Kai Kang, a 29-year-old newspaper vendor, as the director, according to Australian news reports. But Kang's newsstand is in Northern Victoria, over 400 miles from Sydney. Kang's father told Australia's ABC News this week that he had never heard of Megaspeed.

articles.title_orig: The Kraft Group wants to build a $16 billion data center campus in a small Central Mass. town
articles.title_zh: The Kraft Group wants to build a $16 billion data center campus in a small Central Mass. town
articles.content_orig:
New England Patriots owner Robert Kraft’s company is stepping into a political minefield, proposing to build one of the largest data centers in the country in the Central Massachusetts town of Sutton, just as opposition to the facilities is intensifying.
In this area, known for its farmland and home to about 9,700 residents, the Kraft Group would build a massive, $16 billion data center campus. The project would include 10 buildings, erected on land owned by the Krafts’ Unified Packaging box business about 10 miles south of Worcester. It would push Massachusetts into the world of big data centers, as the fourth-biggest facility in the United States, according to the research firm Cleanview.
The proposal must be approved by multiple town committees before moving ahead, and it puts Kraft once again at the center of political controversy , this time as data centers have become political poison across the country . Voters last week from Maine to California approved 44 referendums to block or slow data center construction. Last month, the Western Massachusetts community of Westfield moved to block a large data center proposed there.
The Sutton Select Board met Tuesday night to hear about the project amid a packed hearing room. Chair Jonathan Anderson said the board would not immediately vote on the matter and planned to hold multiple public forums to discuss the proposal with the community.
“This is not a project that’s a done deal,” he said. “It’s far from it. This is the very, very beginning of the process.”
The board allowed only about 15 minutes of public comments at the start of the meeting and all six speakers said they opposed the project. “I would like to see this process stopped tonight,” Sutton resident Sarah Osterman Stone said.
The crowd remained rowdy after the public comments, shouting as the board tried to move on with its business. “Kill it now,” one person shouted. “Just end the process,” another added.
The Sutton proposal would dwarf the Westfield project. When completed in 2033, the Kraft data center would draw 900 megawatts of electricity, enough to power a sizable city. Three larger data centers are already in operation; many larger projects are in the planning or construction stages, including Meta’s 6,500 megawatt data center in Louisiana.
Given the fierce opposition to data center construction and comments at Tuesday’s meeting, the Kraft Group is likely to face strong local opposition. Residents have also been stirring in comments on social media.
“There’s been a pretty quick response from the community expressing concerns,” said state Representative Joe McKenna, who represents the area. The main issues are that the project could drive up electricity rates, consume too much water, and generate noise, he said. “They’re concerns that I share, but I’m also not willing to say ‘No’ just based on a fear of an unknown, or fear of an uncertainty,” McKenna added.
Sutton’s town manager, Austin J. Cyganiewicz, confirmed the $16 billion proposal from the Kraft Group and Unified Global Packaging Group in a letter sent Monday to the town’s Select Board.
The Kraft Group did not return a request for comment Tuesday.
The Krafts clashed last summer with Foxborough town officials over $8 million in security costs for the World Cup. And in September, Robert Kraft drew wide criticism for barring rap artist Macklemore from performing at Gillette Stadium over his remarks in support of Palestinians.
As for the move into data centers, Massachusetts has so far not been an appealing destination for the large, energy-hungry facilities powering the AI boom — Sutton would be the first. That’s because the state has among the highest electricity rates in the country, not to mention high land prices and construction costs, IDC analyst Matt Eastwood said.
But as the AI boom moves from early development to broader usage, every part of the country will need local, large data centers, according to Eastwood.
If approved, the first two buildings at the Sutton site, off Boston and Providence roads, would open in 2029, and two more facilities would come online each year through 2033, for a total of 10.
The Kraft Group did not yet provide information about possible tenants of the data center. But they’re making a bet based on the plans of AI giants like OpenAI and Anthropic, which are expected to spend hundreds of billions of dollars leasing space in such facilities.
Given the forecasts of exploding AI usage, businesses eventually will need nearby data centers to avoid software slowdowns, Eastwood said. “You’ll end up with an AI infrastructure that’s much more distributed and not as centralized,” he said, with a handful of megasized data centers needed in New England.
In parts of the country with numerous data centers, the facilities appear to have driven up electricity rates . The Sutton campus, if fully built, would draw power equal to about 7 percent of the state’s peak usage on the hottest summer day last year.
For the town of Sutton, which is struggling to balance its budget over the next few years, property tax revenue from the data center could win over skeptics.
The full facility would represent a multiple of the $2.8 billion in assessed value of all the property in Sutton, Cyganiewicz wrote.
The first two buildings on the data center campus would pay $10.4 million annually in property taxes starting in fiscal year 2031. That sum would rise to about $27.8 million a year on all 10 buildings in 2035, Cyganiewicz estimated in his letter.
In a town with a $40 million annual budget, that would be a huge windfall, potentially cutting property tax bills for residents by thousands of dollars. An average single-family homeowner in 2031 could see their tax bill fall to $6,846 from $9,134, according to Cyganiewicz.
Still, “the proposal is tentative,” he wrote. “No application has been filed, and important details on power, water, equipment and site impacts are still to come.”
The proposal was previously reported by MassLive.
Data centers have become increasingly controversial as critics point to their environmental impacts, energy consumption, and broader concerns about the effect of artificial intelligence on the job market. Governor Maura Healey in September signed an executive order to block new data centers in Massachusetts unless they get local approval.
US Representative Jim McGovern, whose district includes Sutton, has been a leading opponent of data centers and cosponsored a bill to impose a national moratorium. But McGovern said it would be up to residents to decide whether to move forward with the Kraft proposal.
“Costs of utilities have gone up for a lot of people because the data centers eat up a lot of energy and take a lot of water ... so for me, I don’t like them,” he said. “But, ultimately, it’s up to the people of Sutton.”
Nearly across the board during the midterms, pro-data center candidates backed by Big Tech, including Senate candidates Jon Husted in Ohio and Ken Paxton in Texas, lost.
Many House candidates supporting AI and data centers came up short, too, including Derrick Van Orden in Wisconsin and Rob Bresnahan in Pennsylvania. And in dozens of local referendums around the country, from Wells, Maine, to Defiance, Ohio, and Emporia, Kans., voters approved bans or restrictions on data centers.
Jim Puzzanghera of the Globe staff contributed reporting.
Aaron Pressman can be reached at aaron.pressman@globe.com . Follow him @ampressman . Travis Andersen can be reached at travis.andersen@globe.com .

Windows 11 is getting another substantial batch of changes in November, but after going through what's coming, two improvements stand out to me: the customizable context menu and Cloud Rebuild.
The first finally gives you control over some of the clutter that has plagued Windows 11's right-click menu, while Cloud Rebuild offers a much easier way to reinstall Windows without creating a bootable USB drive.
Those are only two of the 11 changes worth knowing about this month , which also include improvements for handheld gaming, Phone Link , accessibility , Edge performance, security, and more.
Availability will vary because Microsoft rolls many features out gradually , but here's what you should be watching for in our latest Windows 11 guide .
Here's all you need to know about the features and changes coming in November.
Starting with the November update, Windows 11 is getting a new context menu experience that gives you more control over the commands and app extensions that appear in the main menu.
The new menu reduces clutter and makes the experience faster by moving app extensions into a separate submenu. It also introduces a "Customize menu" option at the bottom of the interface, which opens a dedicated Settings page where you can enable or disable built-in commands, add options such as "Print" and "Send to," and control which app extensions appear in the main menu or submenu.
You can also display "Cut," "Copy," "Paste," "Rename," "Delete," and "Share" as individual commands instead of showing them in a vertical view. Windows 11 also lets you move "Properties" to the bottom of the menu as it appeared on Windows 10 .
To access these options, right-click a file, folder, or the desktop and select Customize menu , or open Settings > Personalization > Context menu .
You can keep the default configuration if you prefer. Holding down "Shift" while right-clicking also reveals the legacy context menu.
The ability to customize the menu is particularly useful because it gives users more control over which commands they see without forcing everyone to use the same layout.
Microsoft is also refreshing the Gaming Task View experience in XBOX mode. The updated interface retains the familiar design but adds a navigation bar that makes it easier to access options such as "Exit to Desktop" and "Power Options" using a game controller.
It's a relatively small change, but it makes basic actions easier to navigate using a gaming controller.
The Settings app is getting a few usability refinements. The "Privacy & security" page now groups Location, Microphone, and Camera controls more clearly, making it easier to review these permissions.
Microsoft is also expanding the "Device Info" card on the "Home" page to more markets. Available to users signed in with a Microsoft account, the card provides an overview of key hardware specifications and a shortcut to the "About" page.
The "Storage" page is also getting visual changes to its temporary files section.
These aren't major additions, but they make some commonly used Settings pages easier to navigate.
Phone Link integration is getting a small convenience improvement. When your phone is connected, you can hover over a recent message or notification in the Start menu 's "Recent" section of the mobile pane to preview its contents without opening it.
It's a minor addition, but it makes checking incoming messages more convenient without opening your phone or the Phone Link app.
The Magnifier feature is getting three useful improvements, including independent zoom levels for multiple monitors, viewport locking, and a new contrast theme. These additions give you more control over magnified content while making it easier to work across multiple displays.
The biggest improvement is per-monitor zoom, which lets you assign a different magnification level to each display. For example, you can keep one monitor at 150 percent and another at 200 percent.
The feature is enabled by default, but displays must use "Extend" mode. Adjust each screen with the Magnifier toolbar or shortcuts (" Windows key + Plus/Minus "). Viewport locking keeps one magnified screen fixed while you move the pointer to another. Use " Ctrl + Windows key + K " to lock/unlock or " Windows key + Esc " to release all. A new dark contrast theme reduces glare while keeping colors intact. Enable it from the Magnifier toolbar or Settings > Accessibility > Magnifier. Color inversion is separate.
The Narrator feature now supports reading and navigating math equations, making it easier for people with low vision to understand formulas, equations, and scientific notation.
The feature works with supported Microsoft 365 apps, including Word and PowerPoint, as well as web content in Microsoft Edge and Google Chrome .
You can use it with the "Narrator key + Alt + N" shortcut to enable math navigation, and then use the arrow keys to explore individual parts of an equation. Use the "Esc" key to exit. Math reading supports six languages, including English, German, Spanish, Finnish, and Traditional Chinese.
You can change the language and other preferences under Settings > Accessibility > Narrator > Math reading .
Browser support requires Microsoft Edge version 153.0.4234.32 or later, or Google Chrome version 153.0.8010.18 or later.
Windows 11 is making recovery easier by allowing the Windows Recovery Environment (WinRE) to reuse eligible Wi-Fi profiles saved in the main operating system.
This allows computers to connect automatically to supported wireless networks during recovery operations such as Quick Machine Recovery and Cloud Rebuild, without requiring administrators to configure Wi-Fi credentials separately during recovery.
The feature is enabled by default and supports certain certificate-based enterprise networks, though it doesn't currently support TPM-backed certificate keys. Network administrators can turn off the capability through the Recovery Configuration Service Provider (CSP) .
WinRE only accesses saved network credentials when a recovery operation requires connectivity, rather than maintaining a permanent network connection.
I've been testing Cloud Rebuild , and eliminating the need to create installation media is easily its biggest advantage. However, I also ran into an important limitation: the feature depends on Windows Update having the drivers your PC needs.
Unlike a traditional local reinstall, it doesn't depend on the existing Windows installation or require a bootable USB drive or a custom recovery image. You can also start it from the Windows Recovery Environment when the device cannot boot.
You can start the process under Settings > System > Recovery and use the "Rebuild this PC" option, or from WinRE by selecting Troubleshoot > Recovery and uninstall > Cloud Rebuild . After connecting to Ethernet or Wi-Fi, the system will display the target build, edition, and language before installation.
The feature includes two options to clean the drive. For example, the "Remove files" option reformats the system drive, although specialized recovery tools might still recover some data. On the other hand, the "Remove and sanitize files" option uses the storage hardware's erase capability to eras

articles.title_orig: China’s Nvidia Honeypot Isn’t Surprising. Jensen Huang Fell for It Anyway
articles.title_zh: China’s Nvidia Honeypot Isn’t Surprising. Jensen Huang Fell for It Anyway
articles.content_orig:
Nvidia 's stock rose 3% on Wednesday, after falling for two days amid the scandal that has rocked the world's most valuable tech company.
Shares closed down 5.47% on Tuesday as more details were revealed about the impact of CEO Jensen Huang 's affair with an alleged Chinese spy . They fell 4.3% Monday.
On Tuesday, Nvidia announced it had hired law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz to investigate whether company secrets or national security were compromised.
Huang tried to project "business as usual" as he returned to the office on Monday, people familiar with the matter told CNBC. The CEO was also in the office on Tuesday, conducting meetings, ahead of the company's quarterly earnings on Nov. 17.
Investors are assessing whether the matter will have damaging spillover effects on the business.
In a Tuesday note, Bank of America said it saw three scenarios with differing investment outcomes. In one scenario, the impact is contained with leadership continuity, and in another, prolonged uncertainty pressures valuation before earnings.
In the final scenario, the impact is escalated, with "adverse findings, leadership disruption or tighter restrictions requiring earnings reassessment," BofA research analyst Vivek Arya said in the note.
Zacks' Chief Equity Strategist John Blank said the selloff reflected two concerns: that the U.S. might impose further restrictions in the wake of the affair and that further problems might arise as the news develops. "What else has Jensen done?" he said.
"It's not good for Nvidia. It's not good for Jensen Huang. It's certainly not good for the AI trade," Blank told CNBC's "Squawk Box Europe" on Wednesday.
Morgan Stanley on Wednesday removed Nvidia as a top pick after shares dropped more than 25% since it was named on the list on Oct. 2. Huang's leadership is "crucial" to the company's strategic direction, analysts said in a Wednesday note.
— CNBC's Michael Bloom and Caleigh Keating contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Trump wanted little Kei trucks for America, Toyota makes it happen
articles.title_zh: Trump wanted little Kei trucks for America, Toyota makes it happen
articles.content_orig:
The idea that Americans should be offered a greater choice of smaller cars has support from strange bedfellows indeed. After all, who could forget President Trump—usually one to take a maximalist approach to any problem— announcing last year that he wanted the Department of Transportation to make Japan’s diminutive “Kei” cars legal here in the US.
Ars’ attempts to get DoT to tell us more about the potential influx of little vehicles have mostly fallen on deaf ears. But this week, there has been movement on the topic, with Toyota announcing that it will bring back the Scion brand with the KEI-01.
Here in the US, the preponderance of humongous SUVs is a consequence largely of government policies, specifically corporate average fuel economy standards that made it less profitable to sell smaller, efficient cars. Japan’s Kei cars are what happens if the government instead restricts the size, engine capacity, and power output.
A Kei car must fit within the following dimensions: 11.2 feet (3.4 m) long, 4.9 feet (1.5 m) wide, and 6.6 feet (2 m) tall, with an engine displacement of no more than 0.66 L and an output of 63 hp (47 kW) or less. That’s a far cry from the more than 16 feet (4.9 m) of a full-size pickup truck, but it makes sense for a country where you’re not allowed to buy a car unless you have somewhere to park it, with those spaces being at an absolute premium.
Being affordable to buy and economical to run sure doesn’t hurt either, and last year, Japan bought almost 1.7 million Kei cars, out of total sales of 4.6 million vehicles. Depending on where you live in the US, it can be varying degrees of difficult to import a Kei car , at least until now.
Toyota killed off its Scion sub-brand more than a decade ago , ending the haggle-free approach and cars aimed at younger buyers in favor of selling more Toyotas. But now it’s back as “Scion by Toyota,” which the automaker will apparently use to experiment with less traditional ideas. But forget about a cool-but-boxy EV in the mold of the Honda N-One or Nissan Sakura .
“The future of mobility will not be defined by one vehicle, one technology, or one way of thinking,” said Simon Humphries, Toyota’s chief branding officer and head of design. “Scion by Toyota gives us a place to challenge conventional thinking, explore new possibilities, and create mobility in new ways. The KEI-01, SxS, and BKE concepts each represent a different possibility—and together, they show what can happen when curiosity leads the way.”
Before anyone gets too excited, the KEI-01 will be classified as a “ low-speed vehicle ,” which means it can’t go any faster than 25 mph (40 km/h). So if you were hoping to use one of these but need to drive on anything but surface streets, be prepared to get honked at, a lot, and not in a good way. In fact, unless you’re buying a fleet, Toyota won’t sell you a KEI-01 at all, at least not to begin with.
Oh, and it’s only available as right-hand drive, since that’s the side of the road Japan drives on. But it does feature all-wheel drive, so if you own a ranch—or perhaps a whole load of golf courses—the utility becomes a little more obvious. Toyota says the KEI-01 is suited to small business owners in urban environments, farmers and ranchers, organizations that have campuses that need fleets of facility vehicles, delivery drivers, and outdoor enthusiasts. The trucks will be shipped to Toyota’s assembly plant in Indiana as knock-down kits, adding 50 jobs to the plant in mid-2027.
Low-speed vehicles have been street-legal in parts of the US for many years now. In my neighborhood in Washington, DC, Circuit operates a low-speed EV shuttle on demand, and gas-powered golf carts are very popular in retirement communities. Pricing for the KEI-01 hasn’t been announced, but speculation runs from as little as $10,000 to as much as $28,000.

articles.title_orig: Stock Market Today: Nasdaq Jumps After CoreWeave Earnings
articles.title_zh: Stock Market Today: Nasdaq Jumps After CoreWeave Earnings
articles.content_orig:
Stocks were mostly higher Wednesday, boosted by sharp gains in CoreWeave and a rebound in Nvidia following back-to-back losing sessions for the chipmaker.
The Nasdaq Composite jumped 1.9%, while the S&P 500 advanced 1.3%. The Dow Jones Industrial Average gained 62 points, or 0.1%
Neocloud stock CoreWeave rallied 20% after reporting third-quarter revenue that beat analyst expectations. CoreWeave also lifted operating income and revenue guidance for 2026.
Nvidia, meanwhile, climbed 2.7% after dropping nearly 10% to start the week when CEO Jensen Huang confirmed he had an affair with an alleged Chinese spy. The pullback in Nvidia weighed on the broader market Tuesday, with the major averages ending the session lower.
"The sentiment bump coming from CoreWeave results and Anthropic IPO demand is helping the broader ecosystem," Ross Mayfield, an investment strategist at Baird Private Wealth Management, told CNBC. "Markets are continuing to unwind last week's overshoot to the downside with cleaner positioning now a tailwind and an attractive near-term valuation/earnings story in a lot of the AI stocks."
Artificial intelligence lab Anthropic on Tuesday said in an updated Securities and Exchange Commission filing that it will offer 825 million shares in an initial public offering planned for next week that could value the five-year-old company at as much as $1.4 trillion.
Equities fell on Tuesday after stronger-than-expected October inflation data renewed expectations that the Federal Reserve will again raise interest rates at its final policy meeting of the year in December. The consumer price index increased by 0.4% month over month in October , topping economists' estimates.
Expectations for a quarter-point rate increase next month rose to about 90% following the Dept. of Labor release, according to the CME Group's FedWatch tool.
"Despite some technical uncertainty, higher than desired levels of inflation should keep the Fed in a stance of dissatisfaction with the degree of progress on inflation remaining lackluster, so hiking the Fed Funds policy rate in December is our and the market's base case," wrote Rick Rieder, CIO of global fixed income at BlackRock. "The question now is more of one of the extent of the hike."
Comments from Fed Governor Christopher Waller at a Bank of England conference in London Tuesday also led traders to price in a greater chance of a quarter-point move.
The U.S. bond market is closed on Wednesday for Veterans Day.
Chicago Federal Reserve President Austan Goolsbee called the latest inflation data "borderline disturbing."
"It's another distressing report — borderline disturbing," Goolsbee said in an interview with the PBS NewsHour Tuesday.
"We've got a real inflation issue on our hands that has been developing," Goolsbee said. "We're going to have to deal with that."
The consumer price index rose 0.4% on a seasonally adjusted basis in October, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics' Tuesday morning release. That was higher than economists had predicted, and the third straight month of outsized price increases.
CoreWeave shares jumped 20% Wednesday after the neocloud posted quarterly earnings that beat estimates and raised its guidance for the year.
"Demand for the infrastructure is and remains overwhelming." CEO Michael Intrator told CNBC's "Squawk on the Street" Wednesday.
"I think I said that we are 10x oversubscribed to the existing capacity that we have left in 2027, and we are multiples ... oversubscribed on the capacity we have out in 2028," he said.
Berkshire Hathaway 's "Buffett premium" is evaporating, according to CFRA, citing "eroding fundamentals" and uncertainty around the "significant management transition."
In a Tuesday note, analyst Catherine Seifert highlighted insurance as a "weak spot" in during the firm's third quarter, which reported a decline in operating earnings .
She also mentioned shares of Berkshire "merit caution in the near term." At current levels, the stock trades at about 25 times CFRA's 2026 operating earnings per share, above their three-year average forward multiple of 23 times.
Warren Buffett announced his retirement as CEO at the end of 2025. He remains the chairman emeritus and a Board Director at the firm.
Current CEO Greg Abel, a CPA and the former CEO of MidAmerican Energy, brings "strong operational skills" to this role. Although, he still has big shoes to fill.
Still, Seifert highlighted bright spots, including Berkshire's balance sheet which continues to reflect "solid financial strength" as well as buybacks.
In Q3, the conglomerate bought back $9.6 billion worth of Berkshire stock.
Analysts at JPMorgan upgraded Republic Services to overweight from neutral, raising its price target to $295, implying nearly 19% upside from Tuesday's close.
"We expect solid waste volume growth to inflect to positive in 2027 after three years of negative growth," JPMorgan analyst Tami Zakaria wrote in a Wednesday note.
Small and large container volumes each rose 0.5% in the third quarter this year, marking their first simultaneous growth in more than three years. Zakaria said the recovery will help companywide adjusted EBITDA margins expand at or above the high end of Republic's annual target of 30 to 50 basis points.
Free cash flow should increase in 2028 as Polymer Center construction wraps up, the analyst said. Republic also plans to begin full-scale deployment of its AI-enhanced routing platform in early 2027 to improve collection efficiency and reduce disposal costs.
The company remains on track to generate $100 million in annualized adjusted EBITDA from digital initiatives by the end of 2028, according to Zakaria.
The three major indexes moved higher shortly after the opening bell on Wednesday. The S&P 500 advanced 1%, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average ticked up 45 points, or 0.1%. The Nasdaq Composite gained 1.6%.
Goldman Sachs now expects the Federal Reserve to hike in March as well as in December.
Hotter-than-expected October inflation will help to motivate an additional quarter-point interest rate hike from the Federal Reserve in March following the expected December hike, David Mericle at Goldman Sachs thinks.
Mericle sees the possibility of a January hike after the one in December but thinks March is a safer bet due to easing end-of-year inflation.
"A third hike could come earlier in January, but we think March is a bit more likely because we expect the November and December inflation reports to be softer but then expect larger start-of-the-year price increases amidst ongoing cost pressures to boost inflation in January," Mericle wrote in a Tuesday note to clients.
Inflation increased 0.4% in October. Economists had been expecting a 0.3% increase.
Ulrike Hoffmann-Burchardi, CIO of the Americas at UBS, doesn't think a half-point rate hike will take place.
"Before the inflation print, Federal Reserve Governor Christopher Waller said a core CPI reading of around 0.3% or higher could warrant considering a 50-basis-point hike in December," Hoffmann-Burchardi wrote. "But, we still think FOMC support for a 50bps hike is limited because it could signal a need for more aggressive monetary policy recalibration. For now, our base case remains for 25bps Fed hikes in December and March, with the latest developments bolstering the case for higher rates and raising the risk of more or faster tightening than currently expected."
European chipmakers moved higher on Wednesday.
German semiconductor mainstay Infineon advanced 6.3%, while Dutch chipmaker ASMI was up 5.5%, as Switzerland's ST Microelectronics gained 4%. ASML rose about 3%.
CoreWeave shares jumped 15% in premarket trading Wednesday after the neocloud posted quarterly earnings that beat estimates and raised its guidance for the year.
The three months to Sept. 30 marked a "breakout quarter" for CoreWeave, CEO Michael Intrator said, adding that growth was supported by multiple sources of funding, including financing backed by customer contra

articles.title_orig: JetBlue's CEO has pushed back on creditor fears and is betting on premium to return to profitability
articles.title_zh: JetBlue's CEO has pushed back on creditor fears and is betting on premium to return to profitability
articles.content_orig:
JetBlue Airways is unveiling its new domestic first-class seats Wednesday as more of the country's carriers bet on the premium travel boom to make them profitable again.
JetBlue announced it would offer a domestic first class — BlueFirst — in December 2024 and plans to start flying aircraft with the new seats and full on-board product next month. The carrier is showing off the new cabin at its home hub at John F. Kennedy International Airport on Wednesday. Retrofits will continue during 2027, CEO Joanna Geraghty told CNBC late last month.
The rollout comes as the New York airline tries to stabilize after last posting a profit in 2019Last month, JetBlue executives sought to calm investors after shares in the airline hit a record low following a report that bondholders had contracted restructuring advisors.
"We have no intention, no plans to file for bankruptcy. We are not engaged with any restructuring company," Geraghty told CNBC in an interview on Oct. 27.
Geraghty told CNBC's Phil LeBeau on Wednesday that JetBlue has "met with a few of the creditors over the last couple of weeks as part of ... normal investor engagement." She said the company made it clear to bondholders that JetBlue doesn't need to reorganize.
The airline's shares are up more than 40% this month, more than other passenger carriers, as of midday Wednesday, though they are still off about 11% so far this year.
JetBlue is betting that resilient travel demand, especially for for roomier seats will help fuel its turnaround plan, which aims to get the carrier to an operating profit next year and $1 in adjusted earnings per share in 2028.
Airline executives have said they expect fares to stay elevated next year as they grapple with higher costs, including but not limited to fuel, such as labor and airport fees. Geraghty said Wednesday that even if fuel prices moderate next year, "I don't think fares are going to fall as much as people expect."
Airlines large and small are racing to outfit their cabins with roomier, more expensive seating options to help cover ever-higher costs, from jet fuel to labor to airport operation fees.
For example, a ticket in the new recliner first-class seats between Kennedy Airport and Fort Lauderdale-Hollywood International Airport in Florida is going for $847 roundtrip in the first week of March while standard economy is $446.
On Tuesday, budget carrier Frontier Airlines unveiled its new first class seats, which will take up the first two rows, and said it would outfit its Airbus fleet with premium seating that have extra legroom and in-seat power through row eight. The airline will take out a row of seating on its planes to make the pricier ones fit, chief marketing officer Bobby Schroeter told CNBC in an interview Monday.
JetBlue last month reported it ended the third quarter with $2.2 billion in liquidity and that its unencumbered asset base is now $7 billion, including $2.8 billion in aircraft and engines.
JetBlue had total debt of $8.4 billion as of Sept. 30, the carrier said in its earnings filing.
Geraghty told CNBC last month there is a "fundamental disconnect between the narrative in the bond market and what our financial results actually demonstrate."
When asked then whether JetBlue's eye on keeping costs down includes furloughs, layoffs or buyouts, Geraghty last month said "absolutely not."

articles.title_zh: Aer Lingus Pilots Threatened With Criminal Charges Over Bomb Threat Diversion
articles.content_orig:
Last week, I covered how dozens of flights across Europe were faced with bomb threats . It was clearly a hoax, but these have to be taken seriously, and we saw all kinds of diversions, flight cancelations, and more.
Europe’s largest union representing pilots is now sharing the details of an incident that happened with one of these diversions, whereby an Aer Lingus flight was forced by fighter jets to divert to a French military base. When the pilots weren’t comfortable doing so, they were reportedly threatened with criminal charges.
This incident happened on Thursday, November 5, 2026, and involves Aer Lingus flight EI402, scheduled to operate from Dublin (DUB) to Rome (FCO). The Airbus A320 with the registration code EI-DEH took off at 6:40AM local time, and made its way southeast toward Rome.
The A320 flew for around an hour, and made it just past Paris, when the plane changed heading and prepared to divert. French fighter jets had been deployed to escort the aircraft, and demanded that it divert to a French military base. Specifically, the plane diverted to Évreux-Fauville Air Base (EVX), located in Normandy.
The plane touched down there at 10:05AM local time, 2hr25min after it first departed (there was a one hour time change). Coincidentally, that’s basically the same flight time as it would’ve been to Rome, as the aircraft had to hold for an extended period of time.
The plane ended up returning to Dublin later in the day, departing at 4:59PM local time, and landing in Dublin at 5:20PM local time, after a flight time of 1hr21min. So passengers spent nearly 12 hours on the plane, only to end up back where they started. Man, that’s rough, especially when you consider these A320s don’t have power ports, Wi-Fi, etc.
Here’s where the story gets really interesting , as explained by the European Cockpit Association (ECA), which represents over 44,000 pilots across Europe, including pilots at Aer Lingus. The union is expressing serious concerns about how this incident was handled.
What happened is that the Aer Lingus pilots didn’t want to divert to Évreux-Fauville Air Base, because they didn’t have the necessary operational information and aeronautical charts to land there. They requested a landing at another airport, but were rejected. According to the pilots, they were even threatened with criminal charges if they didn’t divert to the airport as requested.
That’s the point on which the union is sounding the alarm. Let me just quote the union on this:
As representatives of the pilot profession, ECA, IALPA and SNPL fully recognise and appreciate the assistance provided by authorities in responding to these threats and supporting flight crews in bringing their passengers and aircraft to safety.
However, reports indicate that, in certain circumstances, military aircraft have intercepted civilian airliners and directed aircraft commanders to land at specific airports without adequately considering aircrafts’ operational and safety requirements.
According to information received by IALPA, in one recent incident involving an Aer Lingus aircraft, military fighter aircraft directed the flight crew to divert to a military airfield for which they did not have the necessary aeronautical charts and operational information to safely conduct a landing. Despite the flight crew seeking an alternative and more suitable diversion airport, their request was refused.
ECA, IALPA and SNPL are also alarmed by subsequent reports that the pilots were apparently faced by the prospect of possible criminal prosecution for actions that were, at all times, aimed at protecting their passengers, crew and aircraft.
The union emphasizes that the captain of a flight should have the ultimate responsibility for the safety of passengers, crew, and the aircraft, and that the captain is uniquely positioned to assess the operational circumstances and determine the safest course of action, taking account of all relevant factors, including aircraft performance, available aeronautical information, airport suitability, operational limitations, and the availability of emergency assistance on the ground.
The union points out how the prospect of criminal prosecution against pilots exercising their professional judgment in such circumstances risks undermining aviation safety, and the effective cooperation between flight crews and authorities.
An Aer Lingus A320 was recently forced to divert to a military base in France, after the aircraft faced a bomb threat (which also impacted dozens of other flights). Fighter jets reportedly demanded the plane divert to this airport despite objections from the pilots, who felt they didn’t have sufficient operational information and aeronautical charts to land there.
The union representing pilots claims that the pilots were threatened with criminal charges if they didn’t divert there, which the union believes undermines the responsibility that pilots should have over the safety of their aircraft.
I fully side with the pilots and union here. It’s silly to me that a bomb threat that’s an obvious hoax puts pilots in a situation where they don’t feel comfortable landing at, with no alternatives offered.
What do you make of this Aer Lingus pilot situation?

Doesn’t matter if the commercial pilots what not… the military has guns and missiles. You do what you are told at that moment.

This is how it should be played out, you can fight this afterwards, but at that moment the pilots better do what the fight planes tell them to do.
The fighter pilots don't know for sure that it was a hoax, they don't know for sure that the person speaking to them from the plane were the actual pilots.  What they did know was that the pilots were refusing to follow their orders in what could have been a serious situation.  What should they have done?
You see what happens when you threaten logical thinking and diplomacy with missiles and bureaucracy.

Warmongers can learn a thing or two from this.
Key question is, how much further away was the alternative? 

The fact that it ended up being a hoax, does not mean it was being treated as one at the time. Another 10 minutes in the air could have been a disaster. That’s also not to say a fighter jet pilot has a totally different set of skills to a commercial pilot; so shouldn’t be telling them what they’re capable of. All the more so making threats when they say they aren’t capable. It’s like an F1 racer telling a 18 year old in a VW he should be able to take the hairpin at 150mph.
Completely on the pilots side.

articles.title_orig: Micron Is Rebounding but Goldman Prefers These Memory Stocks
articles.title_zh: Micron Is Rebounding but Goldman Prefers These Memory Stocks
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Micron's ( MU ) valuation has reached a level where it's simply too cheap to ignore given its fundamentals, says Goldman Sachs analyst James Schneider.
Schneider reiterated his $1,250 price target on the once red-hot AI momentum trade. It assumes about 70% upside from current levels.
"We also believe risk/reward is becoming more attractive for Neutral-rated Micron in light of the high probability of strong free cash flow in the coming quarters," Schneider said.
Micron is currently approaching tangible book value, Schneider noted. When a stock trades below tangible book value, investors value the company at less than the estimated value of its assets after subtracting its liabilities and intangible assets.
In a sense, the market is saying the company's physical and financial assets are worth more than the entire company's stock market value.
That seems to be bordering on an unwarranted disconnect , at least in assessing Schneider's work on the chip player.
Micron's stock is down 17% over the past month amid fears that a blue wave on Election Day could slow the build-out of AI infrastructure. That could have ramifications for orders for Micron's memory chips.
The rout has brought Micron's forward price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio down to an almost laughable 4.2 times, according to Yahoo Finance AlphaSpace data. Keep in mind Micron is coming off a quarter of strong demand amid memory chip shortages driving up prices.
The Street still expects Micron to grow earnings by at least 17% in its next fiscal year.

articles.title_orig: Pope Leo returns to Peru, his adopted homeland
articles.title_zh: Pope Leo returns to Peru, his adopted homeland
articles.content_orig:
Lee el artículo en español
Riding on horseback to visit the most isolated Andean areas of his community, distributing food amid the Covid-19 pandemic, or wearing rubber boots in the water and mud of floods: this is how many Peruvians remember the man who is now Pope Leo XIV.
Robert Prevost was in the trenches and alongside his people during Peru’s most difficult moments, and many of these memories will likely be front of mind among the public as they welcome the pope on his visit to his adopted homeland on Wednesday — a trip that will include visits to Lima, Cusco, Chiclayo and several other cities.
A young Prevost first arrived in the South American country as a missionary in 1985. The years that followed shaped his leadership style, which would later lead him to become the successor to the late Pope Francis.
“I think he was heroic in many ways; he risked becoming ill. We lost 11 priests and a bishop emeritus during that time,” Father José Del Rosario recalls of the most difficult days of the pandemic.
Padre Robert, as he is known in Spanish in Peru, traveled more than 700 kilometers (435 miles) from Chiclayo to the Diocese of Callao, a province bordering the capital, Lima, where he served as apostolic administrator.
“He came every two weeks in his little car; he came alone in a simple pickup truck,” explained Del Rosario, parish priest and rector of the Sanctuary of Our Lady of Mount Carmel of La Legua, who worked closely with the then-bishop.
Pope! Amigo! Peruvians remember the young American priest who became pope
Prevost distributed food and everything needed by a population that lived under lockdown for months, while also offering spiritual guidance during the crisis.
“He gave us a lot of hope and cared for our people, a man who was very close to the people … and also very humble,” Del Rosario added.
Peru recorded more than 219,000 deaths , according to Johns Hopkins University figures, and one of the highest coronavirus mortality rates in the world. In Lima, and especially in the regions, terrifying scenes unfolded outside hospitals, with sick people collapsing in the street due to the shortage of oxygen, one of the key tools for treating the virus.
In Chiclayo, Bishop Prevost launched a fundraising campaign to purchase an oxygen plant. Together with Caritas Chiclayo, the bishop appealed to authorities and sectors of civil society and managed to raise more than US$380,000 for not just one but two oxygen plants.
Janinna Sesa, former director of Caritas Chiclayo, worked with the bishop for eight years, including during the pandemic, the flooding caused by the coastal El Niño in 2017, and Cyclone Yaku in 2023.
“We were always on the front lines, especially during disasters like the coastal El Niño phenomenon. He was the person who put on his boots and waded into the water; he helped people. He was very approachable and very kind,” Sesa told CNN.
Before leaving for Rome in 2023, after the late Pope Francis appointed him prefect of the Dicastery for Bishops and president of the Pontifical Commission for Latin America, Bishop Prevost also led appeals for aid for the more than 10,000 people affected by flooding caused by Cyclone Yaku in the north of the country.
“I ask you to be generous; I ask you to open your hearts so that we can help one another and move forward, as we have done in other times of crisis,” Prevost said in a video while standing in the water in the district of Illimo, in the Lambayeque region.
The assistance and response led by Prevost in the face of the massive arrival of Venezuelan migrants in 2018 was comprehensive and had a different vision from that of the country’s other regions.
Peru received more than 1.6 million Venezuelans through November 2025, the second-highest number in the region after Colombia. More than 20,000 of them passed through Chiclayo, and more than 3,500 families settled in the region, according to figures from the Commission for Human Mobility and Human Trafficking of the Diocese of Chiclayo. Prevost also promoted this commission to assist migrants and combat human trafficking.
First American pope marks July 4 on migrant island with plea for ‘compassion and generosity’
“The migration flow descended upon us, with thousands of migrants out on the streets, sleeping there, and the parishes serving as shelters,” Sesa recalled.
Father Robert was concerned not only with providing food and collecting clothing, blankets, and medicine, but also with building the San Vicente de Paúl village, which took them in at Puerto Etén.
“His simplicity, the peace he conveys, that serenity Monsignor Prevost had when listening to people — I still see it in Pope Leo XIV…. He welcomed us with such warmth, with so much love,” Lisbeth Díaz, a Venezuelan resident of Chiclayo and member of the Commission for Human Mobility and Human Trafficking, told CNN.
Prevost prioritized regularizing their legal status so they could work and integrate into society.
Prevost created spaces for dialogue and encouraged many people to raise their voices to denounce abuses during the internal conflict the country experienced beginning in the 1980s and to openly discuss the social reality during the authoritarian regime of the late President Alberto Fujimori in the 1990s.
At the Augustinian mission in Trujillo, the current pontiff and his seminarians traveled through towns and parishes in Andean areas, staging dramatizations that reflected the violence faced by peasants to encourage conversations that would help heal the trauma and pain they had suffered.
Prevost also participated in collecting signatures for the creation of the Truth and Reconciliation Commission (TRC), which investigated the violence between 1980 and 2000 and human rights abuses, particularly in rural Peru. Trujillo and the parishes led by the current pontiff collected the largest number of signatures.
Leo XIV is a pope forged in Peru. The nearly two decades he spent in the land he adopted as his own profoundly shaped his ministry and set him on the path to the papacy. As a bishop, Prevost was a pastor close to his flock, and at the Vatican, one of his closest collaborators is the Reverend Edgard Rimaycuna, a native of Chiclayo.
His work in South America and his leadership of the Order of Saint Augustine caught the attention of Pope Francis, who first appointed him bishop of Chiclayo and later brought him to Rome, where he went on to hold one of the most important positions in the Vatican and also became a cardinal. This made him a candidate in the 2025 conclave.
Pope Leo presides at biggest Mass of his papacy in Buenos Aires, drawing 2.5 million crowd
In the past, the election of an American pope was considered impossible, given that the College of Cardinals did not wish to associate the papacy with the dominant political and cultural power. However, the cardinals who voted for Cardinal Robert Prevost in the 2025 conclave did not see him simply as a candidate from the United States. His experience in Peru garnered broad consensus among the cardinals, who chose a bishop with roots in Latin America — someone who speaks Spanish fluently and is attuned to the concerns of the people of that continent.
The pope’s visit to Peru is widely seen as a homecoming for a pontiff who is a Peruvian citizen and who knows the country in depth.
Reverend John Lydon, a priest and member of the same Augustinian religious order to which the pope belongs, and who lived and worked with Prevost for a decade, told CNN: “I believe his dedication to the poor and his defense of human rights will continue to define his visit.”

articles.title_orig: As higher prices seep into broader economy, Fed officials consider faster hikes
articles.title_zh: As higher prices seep into broader economy, Fed officials consider faster hikes
articles.content_orig:
WASHINGTON — More evidence this week of hot inflation in the U.S. was unpleasant news for the Federal Reserve, not to mention consumers: Rising prices may be spreading beyond the one-time shocks from tariffs and high gas prices into the wider economy, meaning that mortgages, credit cards and other forms of borrowing are likely to become increasingly expensive.
Tuesday's consumer price index report showed broadly rising costs across a range of goods and services, some with little connection to more expensive oil and gas or surging investment in artificial intelligence data centers, another factor blamed for worsening inflation. And there is increasing anxiety among Fed officials that higher oil prices stemming from the Iran war may last longer than previously thought.
A key issue debated by Fed policymakers for months has been whether inflation would cool on its own if the Iran war ended and oil prices fell and as the impact of tariffs faded. But government data suggested inflation rose to 4% in October compared with a year ago, up from 3.7% in September, even as gas prices leveled off.
The potential consequences of the new inflation data emerged immediately. Two Fed officials suggested Tuesday that the central bank may have to hike its key interest rate more quickly to tame inflation. Bigger or faster hikes by the Fed would mean that buying a house or a car, or paying off a credit card would become a steeper hill to climb, with millions of Americans already struggling to make ends meet.
Lorie Logan, president of the Federal Reserve Bank of Dallas and a voting member of the Fed's rate-setting committee, said Tuesday that price increases remain high for services such as "visits to the doctor, childcare, dining out and hotel stays."
"Prices for these services aren't particularly sensitive to tariffs, conflict in the Middle East or surging demand for computer chips," she added. "While I expect inflation to moderate as price pressures dissipate in energy and manufactured goods, the broader inflationary trend is more likely to persist."
Logan said Tuesday she supported two additional quarter-point rate hikes. While she has made similar statements before, Logan added that the Fed could "move more rapidly this winter" than it "has moved so far this fall," signaling that she may support two rate hikes in a row, a quicker pace than the Fed's current approach.
At its last meeting in late October, the central bank kept rates unchanged at about 3.9%. Chairman Kevin Warsh declined to suggest whether more increases were likely. The central bank hiked rates at its September meeting.
Wall Street investors now see 90% odds that the Fed will lift borrowing costs at its next meeting Dec. 8-9, according to futures prices tracked by CME Fedwatch . Expectations for a second hike at its January meeting tripled between Monday and Tuesday, to more than 64%.
Some Fed officials had expressed optimism over the summer that once the shocks from tariffs and high gas prices faded, inflation would retreat without Fed intervention.
But Anna Paulson, president of the Philadelphia Fed, poured cold water on that view in a speech late Tuesday.
"Underlying inflation is above target, and it hasn't come down," she said. "That tells me that elevated inflation isn't just about factors that will go away on their own." Still, she also said she supported only gradual rate increases.
Tuesday's inflation report showed prices rising in many areas with little connection to energy costs or AI, including streaming video services, beef and auto insurance.
But surging investment in data centers has driven up the cost of computer chips, power generation equipment, and copper, among other components, with little sign of easing. Prices for smartphones jumped 1.4% just from September to October, the government said, the largest such increase on record.
Computer prices leapt 0.5% last month, and television prices rose 3.3%, reversing the more typical trend in which those prices fall with technological innovation.
The Fed's focus on inflation's spread isn't entirely new. In late August, Chairman Kevin Warsh called attention to data showing that most goods and services were experiencing notable price increases. His speech at the Fed's Jackson Hole symposium signaled that the central bank would hike rates for the first time in three years the following month.
There has been little improvement in inflationary trends since then. On Tuesday, even before October's inflation figures were released, Fed governor Christopher Waller noted in a speech in London that 70% of services prices rose by 3% or more in September from a year earlier.
Waller also said that if monthly core inflation — which excludes food and energy prices — were to reach 0.3% or higher in October, the Fed should consider a half-point interest rate increase next month, double the size of the usual hike.
As it turned out, that's exactly how much core inflation increased.
Even as oil prices have fallen steadily since the beginning of the month as President Donald Trump has suggested fighting could end in the Middle East, Waller noted that energy costs in the U.S. could remain high.
The cost of insuring oil tankers traveling through the Strait of Hormuz and taking other steps to avoid attacks has added as much as $20 to $30 a barrel to oil prices, Waller said. Diesel fuel prices will also likely stay high because of a lack of refining capacity, some of which has been destroyed in the Ukraine war, he added.
And while the price of a barrel of oil has slid more than 5% over the last 30 days, it still costs about $30 more than it did at this time last year.
In a Tuesday speech at the Council on Foreign Relations, Fed governor Michelle Bowman suggested that inflation may be getting worse, saying that, "price pressures had been concentrated in a few categories, but the latest data suggest that these pressures may be broadening."
